extracted.intended_audience: students, translators, scholars of classical literature and poets/critics applying Aristotelian poetics
extracted.subtask_description: Extract and apply Aristotle’s criteria for composing and evaluating poetry and drama (esp. tragedy and epic), as explained and exemplified in Margoliouth’s edition and introduction to the Poetics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Esoteric style: brevity, technicality, interdependence
rubrics_metrics.description: The Poetics (an esoteric work) displays brevity, technical vocabulary and interdependence with other Aristotelian texts, making it unintelligible without prior study or oral instruction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Brevity may compress meaning to syllables/letters (cf. Panini); technical terms assume other parts of the system; many assertions require cross-reference to Aristotle’s other works (Metaphysics, Rhetoric, Topics, Physics, Ethics) or oral glosses. Anti-pattern: treating the Poetics as a self-contained popular manual; expecting clarity without knowledge of the wider Aristotelian corpus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Origin of poetry: mimicry plus harmony and rhythm
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry arises from two definite causes: Mimicry (imitation) together with Harmony and Rhythm; these latter belong to order and are 'according to nature.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose by imitating action/agents and by organizing material with order, harmony and rhythm. Use order/rhythm/harmony deliberately since they aid perception and operations (infants delight in them; they are 'according to nature').

rubrics_metrics.name: Create illusion/credibility via concomitant detail (use of signs)
rubrics_metrics.description: When a fiction suggests something that would, if real, be accompanied by other natural signs, include those concomitant details so the audience wrongly infers the fiction's reality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Homer’s Bath-scene detail (tears/gesture) functions as a sign that leads the mind to accept the fiction. Practical rule: add plausible attendant facts or sensory details that would naturally accompany the central fictional fact to produce belief/illusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use 'ordinary language' and common usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Difficulties in poetic diction are often solved by appealing to ordinary language and customary usage; poetic naming can follow common practice (e.g., calling a diluted mixture 'wine' when the dominant element gives form).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer usages and names that align with familiar, conventional categorizations (form/matter logic). Anti-pattern: forcing unnatural neologisms or technicalized diction when ordinary idiom serves the portrayal and recognizability of things.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of dramatic (unity of action): beginning, middle and end
rubrics_metrics.description: A dramatic work should have a beginning, middle and end — unity of theme/action — so that the whole forms a coherent, ordered sequence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct plots with clear initiation, development and termination; avoid loose episodic arrangements. Homer is credited with discovering this principle. Scoring note: evaluate whether incidents are arranged to form a single, intelligible whole rather than an assortment of episodes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primacy of plot: poet as fabricator of story not only of verse
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet (fabricator) ought primarily to fabricate stories (plots) rather than merely produce good verse; the artistic form of the story is central.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize construction of action/incident and causal structure over metrical ornament. Anti-pattern: prioritizing verbal prettiness while plot is disjointed or unmotivated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid deus ex machina and unprepared solutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Resolutions or 'solutions' (e.g., deus ex machina) that are not prepared by antecedent incidents are criticized; a solution must be consistent with the play’s antecedents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure that outcomes and appearances of characters are naturally supported by prior plot material. Example discussion: Medea’s chariot vs. Aegeus—Aristotle locates fault where the solution is not foreshadowed. Anti-pattern: introducing extraneous devices late to tidy the plot without causal groundwork.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragedy’s theme: portrayal of persons functioning (teleia praxis) and link to happiness
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy portrays persons of extraordinary virtue engaged in action (praxis telera/energeia); the theme is related to 'life and happiness' and often involves a transition from good fortune to ill fortune.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shape tragic plots around meaningful actions of characters whose fortunes and moral functioning bear on the theme of happiness and its loss; grounding tragedy in Aristotelian ethical/metaphysical concepts clarifies stakes. Anti-pattern: treating tragedy as mere spectacle without coherent moral/teleological import.

rubrics_metrics.name: Order, harmony and rhythm as natural causes of aesthetic effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Order (including harmony and rhythm) is a natural cause of poetic effect — operations are aided by them and they are pleasing 'according to nature.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use ordered arrangement of parts, rhythmic patterns and harmonious structures to enhance perception and aesthetic response. Reference other texts when justifying why order works (Physics, Problems, Arbeit und Rhythmus).

rubrics_metrics.name: Character defined by action and relative moral categories
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters are to be classified in terms of actions and moral qualities (virtue/viciousness) — often relative to standards (balanced alternatives) rather than absolute exclusive categories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portray characters through what they do (actions) and understand virtue/viciousness as relative to a norm; avoid treating characters as absolutely only 'good' or 'bad' without relational context. Anti-pattern: one-dimensional moral caricature that ignores relative standards and roles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interdependence of argumentative/terminological framework (expect cross-textual concepts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Many terms and points in the Poetics presuppose doctrines explained elsewhere (e.g., Topics, Metaphysics, De Anima, Ethics); one should expect and supply cross-referential explanations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When applying Aristotelian criteria, be prepared to bring in related concepts (forms, categories, energeia, definitions of happiness, standard of comparison) to interpret terms; for modern use, footnote or explicate such presuppositions to readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid episodic structure; ensure causal interconnection
rubrics_metrics.description: An 'episodic' tragedy (disconnected incidents) is bad; incidents must follow by natural or probable causal relations to form unity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arrange scenes so each incident derives from or causes others; test whether a supposed episode could be removed without harming the whole. Anti-pattern: assembling striking scenes without causal or thematic ties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate rôle and integration of the Chorus
rubrics_metrics.description: The Chorus must be used in a way that serves the dramatic structure; misuse or transplanting of choral songs is criticized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Integrate choric odes functionally: their placement, content and relation to action should support unity and emotional effect. Anti-pattern: borrowing choric material from elsewhere or using the Chorus as irrelevant ornament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of disclosure (anagnorisis), reversal (peripeteia) and irony as devices
rubrics_metrics.description: Devices such as disclosure (recognition), reversal of fortune and the irony of fate are important tools for producing tragic effect when properly prepared and integrated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ recognition and reversal only when antecedents make them credible; these devices should deepen thematic meaning (e.g., Oedipus’s discovery providing compressed tragic unity). Anti-pattern: contrived surprises with no prior indication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate compression/expansion for medium (tragedy vs epic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Different genres require different treatment of scale and compression: tragedies tend to be compressed (e.g., Oedipus) while epics like the Iliad are more expansive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match narrative scope and compression to the medium’s needs: compress where unity of action and concentrated moral impact are required; expand where breadth and multiplicity of incidents suit the form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Picture-specific detail preferred for effect (Homeric picturesque detail)
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific, picturesque details (as Homer’s practice) are valuable: they supply vivid signs that support the illusion and help audience inference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ particularized sensory images and small behavioral details to make scenes convincing and to cue readers’ inferences about characters and events. Anti-pattern: abstract or generic description that fails to activate the reader’s inference machinery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logical/formal precision in terminology and alternatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Understand and use Aristotle’s logical formulas correctly (e.g., 'balanced alternatives' vs 'exhausted alternatives'); distinctions affect interpretation of claims about character and action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When invoking claims like 'either virtuous or vicious', distinguish whether Aristotle means relative to a standard (balanced alternatives) or exclusive categorization (exhausted alternatives). Misreading logical form leads to mistaken criticism or emendation.
